subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING PASSPORTS-REPAYMENT OF FEES- STAFF OVERTIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I promised
the other day that I would make a brief statement on the passport situation. The passport office is going through its peak period-12,500 applications were received last week-and the present volume of applications is expected to continue with only slight easement until mid June.
I realize that this situation has created inconvenience for some members of the travelling public, and the following measures have been taken to cut down the delays:
(a)	We are in the process of adding additional accommodation to the passport office which will improve the efficiency of operations and provide room for additional staff. Simultaneously as the program of renovation proceeds, we are adding additional staff;
(b)	Nine departmental staff who in the past have had experience in passport work have been drafted on a temporary basis. In addition, during the course of the next two weeks some 27 students who worked in the passport office last summer will be returning to their jobs;
(c)	The passport office staff has increased its daily overtime and will work Saturday until the present situation is resolved. The implementation of this policy takes into account individual staff problems, and we hope that Saturday work will not be required beyond the present week.
(d)	Three additional telephone lines, for a total of six, have been installed in the special ternoon, has been on the amendment moved
(e)	The staff of examiners has been reorganized in groups of five, each working under a leader. During the course of this week each group leader will be equipped with a telephone. If a form is not properly filled, he will be able to speak to the applicant by telephone to let him know what more information or documentation is required. This should cut down on time consuming exchanges of correspondence;
(f)	During the course of a few days I intend to launch an advertising campaign to assist the public to obtain passports without undue delay.
May I add that all applicants could assist the passport office by initiating their applications at an early date, by taking greater care

April 30, 1969
External Affairs
in the completion of their applications, and by insuring that they have submitted the necessary documentation, photos and fee.
I should perhaps add answers to a couple of questions that were asked me and which I promised to answer. The first was a question about the repayment of refunding of fees to persons who cannot obtain requisite service or who cannot obtain their passports. If the passport office is unable to issue a passport for various reasons, or an applicant fails within a reasonable period to reply to a request for additional information or documentation to substantiate his entitlement, the fee is automatically refunded after due warning by two follow-up letters.
If an applicant informs the passport office that he is forced to cancel his travel plans, photographs and any documents submitted will be returned and the fee refunded. If in such a case an application has reached the stage in production where the document is being prepared, or already has been issued, the document is however forwarded. I suggest that at this stage it would be unreasonable for the passport office to refund the fee in view of the administration costs that have been invested. In any event, the passport when issued is normally valid for five years. The chances are, therefore, that the cancelled trip might be taken in the season or in an ensuing year.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
There was also a question about payment of overtime to the staff of the passport office. There is no authorization to pay clerical employees for overtime at rates higher than those already established by the Treasury Board. When collective bargaining agreements have been ratified by the union membership, overtime will be compensated at time and a half and employees working on Sundays and holidays will be paid at a higher rate.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING PASSPORTS-REPAYMENT OF FEES- STAFF OVERTIME
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING PASSPORTS-REPAYMENT OF FEES- STAFF OVERTIME
speechtext:
I think Members of Parliament will agree that despite all the difficulties under which they work the employees of the passport office have shown patience in the face of what amounts to intolerable working conditions and hours. It is because the passport office enjoys such a low priority-I say this with great frankness-in the affairs of the department, that these conditions have not been remedied long ago.

I hope that when the minister begins his advertising campaign people will be told in plain language how to go about obtaining not only birth certificates but citizenship. There has been a crisis in this division for some months. Many hon. members have hesitated to raise this matter, feeling that to do so might only add to the problems which the overworked division is experiencing. I am glad the minister has finally recognized that conditions are altogether intolerable. Members of all parties have been subjected to forceful importuning over the last few months by citizens whose mail, telegrams or telephone calls have not been answered by the passport office.
I regret the program did not include the simple step of opening offices in other cities in Canada, as announced by the government some months ago. Heaven knows, there are plenty of facilities in our major cities for the receipt of passport applications. The government might follow the example set for some years in the United Kingdom, by decentralizing its passport system so that people could obtain passports in many places across Canada.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING PASSPORTS-REPAYMENT OF FEES- STAFF OVERTIME
speechtext:
The calm statement we have just heard from the minister belies the absolute chaos which exists in the passport office at this moment. We are facing an emergency situation and the government has been caught completely unprepared.
It is a situation which is intolerable. There are more people travelling today than ever, and these people are being seriously inconvenienced. At every airport in this country there are cases of passengers waiting for passports which have not arrived and which will not arrive.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING PASSPORTS-REPAYMENT OF FEES- STAFF OVERTIME
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING PASSPORTS-REPAYMENT OF FEES- STAFF OVERTIME
speechtext:
I do not know the reason for those comments from members on the other side. Apparently they do not admit there is any kind of urgency here, though I believe every member of this house knows that there is an emergency. Indeed there is a tendency for this house to bog down because Members of Parliament are almost totally occupied looking after passport problems. Something has to be done about this.
I was over at the passport office yesterday, and the way in which those girls have to
April 30, 1969

Questions
work under existing conditions is absolutely inhuman. How those girls can stand it, I don't know. Telephones are ringing and the girls are running around. The more confusion that exists, the fewer passports issued. No relief is in sight as far as I can see.
The idea of regional offices, whatever their merit may be, does not offer any solution; I wonder whether it could be a solution anyway. In regard to unemployment insurance the government asked the public to use the mails. It is now talking of reversing the process.
I do not think that the government does have a policy or has one clue about what to do in this situation. The minister talks of refunding the money paid for passports. Is he also going to refund the money people lose because they could not make a charter flight? There are more significant expenditures involved than just the passport fee.
The passport office was designed to operate at a nice, leisurely pace. That leisurely pace has now disappeared. I hope the minister will reply to the suggestion that an emergency does exist, and that he appoint an emergency controller for the passport office immediately to investigate what the problem in the office is, and get the situation cleared up. The minister's statement today is not one designed to instil any confidence for the future.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING PASSPORTS-REPAYMENT OF FEES- STAFF OVERTIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if we were not aware of the facts in respect of the passport problem, we could believe that the opinions expressed by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat are exaggerated. But, it happens that we have had to help several persons to obtain their passports. We, of the Ralliement Creditiste, are experiencing the same difficulties and we must address the same criticisms to the minister because he has not taken in time the necessary steps to prevent such occurrences.
On the other hand, we are not blaming the officials of the passport office who, up to now, have fully co-operated with us.
However, since there has been in the last few months such an increase in the number of applications for passports, the minister's statement was, I think, too long in coming. We also believe that he did not resort to the proper means to alleviate the situation, because the problem is growing worse every month.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):

subtopic: LAW OF THE SEA LEGISLATIVE CHANGES
speechtext:
1. Canada has not taken any specific legislative action as a result of becoming a signatory to the Final Act of the 1958 United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea. However, in 1964 Parliament passed the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act which took into account certain provisions of the 1958 Geneva Convention on the Territorial Sea and Contiguous Zone. This statute also necessitated the passage of certain consequential amendments to the Aeronautics Act, the Canada Shipping Act, the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act, the Criminal Code, the Customs Act and the Fisheries Act. Certain provisions of the Geneva Convention on the Territorial Sea are also reflected in the Oil Pollution Regulations of September,
1968.
2.	Canada's territorial sea has been defined by the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act and also by an initial list of geographical coordinates for the establishment of straight baselines pursuant to Order-in-Council P.C. 1967-2025 of October 26, 1967.
3.	It is presumed that the term "inland waters" refers to the internal waters of Canada. Pursuant to the 1964 Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act these include the waters on the landward side of the baselines of the territorial sea of Canada. These waters have been defined in the same manner described in the reply to part 2 above.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Order.

I thank you very much to have called the members to order, Mr. Speaker, because we must consider such an important bill as earnestly as possible. Some members may not take this bill too seriously. As far as we are concerned, we feel that this bill as well as the amendments
Criminal Code moved these past days are of the utmost importance.
That is why we study them so carefully and so seriously. We put forward every argument we can possibly find, including some opinions expressed by experts and by the public at large who may unfortunately be governed in a few months' time by so odious a bill.
Yesterday, we were discussing amendment No. 27 proposed by the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise), and pertaining to abortion in the case of a female person, pregnant, of full age or married, or of a person under age provided she gets the written consent of her parents or guardian.
The amendment provides that a female person under age who would be pregnant must obtain her father's consent for abortion.
Parental authority over minor children has always been widely recognized in all areas. When the father is deceased, the consent of the mother or the guardian is required; that goes for driver's permits and for the right to enter liquor stores.
The father must always remain the guide, the protector of his minor child, male as well as female. I base my argument on the Civil Code which clearly establishes the responsibility of the father, the mother or the tutor if the father is dead or cannot act.
At page 215 of the Civil Code, and more particularly at section 1053 dealing with offences and quasi-offences, it can be read and I quote:
Every person capable of discerning right from wrong is responsible for the damage caused by his fault to another, whether by positive act, imprudence, neglect or want of skill.
Section 1054 of the Civil Code of the province of Quebec as well as similar provisions in the Common Law clearly establish, and in a more detailed manner, the parents' responsibility towards minor children. Section 1054 reads as follows:
He is responsible not only for the damage caused by his own fault, but also for that caused by the fault of persons under his control and by things he has under his care.
The father, or, after his decease, the mother, is responsible for the damage caused by their minor children;
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that the parents have authority over their children and are responsible for them. What is beyond me is that the amendment of the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) corrects the Civil Code.

April 30, 1969
Criminal Code
Under the above-mentioned clauses, the Civil Code recognizes the authority of the father, but the Criminal Code, as the result of the proposal made today, abolishes the authority of the father over his minor child.
That is why I feel the amendments on abortion are an infringement of the Criminal Code on the Civil Code. It is an infringement of the federal government on the authority of the provinces and by accepting the amendment of the hon. member for Abitibi, we would confirm the paternal authority conferred by the Civil Code.
As for abortion, the amendment if adopted would have for effect to show that the Criminal Code cannot destroy what is already recognized by the Civil Code. The Civil Code establishes the authority of the father over his minor children, but at the present time the Criminal Code does not require the father's consent to the abortion of his female children.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) should be told, once more, that if he does not accept this amendment, he will be violating the constitution which provides the provinces with the authority in civil matters. Thus, he is creating the proper environment for separatism in the provinces.
Moreover, section 186 of the Criminal Code states and I quote:
Every one is under a legal duty as a parent, foster parent, guardian or head of a family, to provide necessaries of life for a child under the age of sixteen years;
Thus, the Criminal Code holds a head of a family criminally responsible for not providing necessaries of life for his children under age. Thus, a head of a family would be held criminally responsible if one of his children under age died of hunger.
On that point, the Criminal Code is clear. If the Minister of Justice were willing to accept the amendment moved by the hon. member for Abitibi, once more we would be confirming the father's authority with regard to abortion.
Section 186 of the Criminal Code indicates that a person is fully grown up at the age of sixteen years. We have ample documentation showing when maturity begins.
On page 262 of a book entitled Adolescence, there is some definition indicating when a child can be considered mature.

If under the terms of the Criminal Code, one allows a 14, 15 or 16-year-old girl to have an abortion, it is obvious that this right is given to someone who is not yet capable of judging all the implications of her act.
Here are other reasons why we ask that the father's consent be compulsory for the abortion of a pregnant girl. The father should have his say regarding children under age.
A girl under age who would not have to get her father's consent will use every possible means to conceal her love affairs from him; she will take all the necessary steps for her abortion because she wants to hide the truth from her father.
The father should have the right to consent to the abortion of a girl under age, otherwise he will be unaware of those facts, and thus the girl will be encouraged to carry on in the same foolish way and make the same mistakes. Why? Because she does not yet have all the required knowledge and is still unaware of the full implication of her responsibilities in connection with life.
I hope that the bill will not be passed without this amendment being agreed upon, for if we granted as much freedom to children under 21, it would mean giving them the green light to lead a loose life that leads to moral decay. Nobody will be able to supervise the young girls who are still unaware of all the responsibilities of life and have their own way without their father's consent.
We claim, Mr. Speaker, that this amendment is in order. If it were not adopted, then there would exist a contradiction between the Civil Code in which the fathers' responsibility towards his child under 21 is made clear and the Criminal Code which for the time being does not enable young girls to consult their father in order to be allowed to undergo abortion.

Many other reasons could be put forward to justify the fact that the father should be consulted when a girl under 21 wants to undergo abortion.
I could quote a few cases which unfortunately arose. In fact, young girls or other persons have induced young girls to undergo abortion so as to obtain a better share of the estate, to inherit greater amounts of money. I would not like this afternoon to deal with all these matters for my hon. colleagues will be able to throw much more light on the facts than I.
I would like to remind the Minister of Justice of the fact that if we adopt the bill in its present state, the provinces will have the right to state that the Criminal Code abolishes the authorithy of the father vested in him by the civil law of the provinces.

Some people may accuse us once more of indulging in witch-hunting and of getting lost in the meandering considerations of past centuries, but it is not by accusing usi of being mediaeval that they will clear up problems as old as the world itself.
If the daughters' of Adam and Eve had had the freedom to dispose of the foetuses nestling in their womb, where would mankind be?
On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, the fruit of their love was of such a value that never would they have thought, even for a second, to get rid of it. They may have regretted the apple but never this fertilized ovum which was intensely wanted through one of the deepest instincts the Creator has ever instilled in the soul, one which is irresistibly manifested in the body by the ineffable sensual pleasure linked to the function of reproduction.
This instinct has been transmitted in full. This explains the existence of the world. Without doubt, it happened one day that a pervert came to sully this unescapable natural law. I would tend to think that this sad individual was a descendent of Cain.

However, the effects of abortion are often detrimental to women and create guilt and hostility complexes in the mother and this is often worse than what can be obtained by abortion, or than the secondary psychiatric or psychological reactions due to an unwanted pregnancy.

To help the doctors understand more clearly the situation of a girl under age and whose problem is now under study, I would say that it is important that the doctor consulted should have the consent of the parents or guardians. There is at the present time a considerable body of psychiatric opinion which states that it is impossible to prove that either neurosis or psychosis can be prevented by abortion. This has been illustrated in several studies.

The government thought it was an astute policy to introduce this bill immediately after the Easter recess claiming that an immediate debate was necessary, and leading us to believe that we had to rush the passage of that bill in order to proceed to more urgent measures. We shall certainly not be fooled by such a childish game. Indeed, we are not deprived of intelligence to such an etxent. We were opposed to this debate and we have been proving, for the past two weeks, that it was useless.

Mr. Speaker, the many points of orders and questions of privilege which have been raised in the course of this debate have probably led me to make this digression and I do apologize for it. In any case, I promise I will do my best to be as brief as possible and to limit myself to 20 minutes.
Mr. Speaker, the amendment raises the question of accrediting the hospitals.
Should, this bill be adopted as a whole, we want to reduce as much as possible the harmful effects of abortion. We think that by reducing the number of hospitals where it would be possible to perform abortion and by setting the conditions under which these hospitals might be accredited for that purpose, we would have successfully dealt with one of
Criminal Code
the many means of alleviating its evil consequences.
Mr. Speaker, if we look at the amendment from this point of view, we can understand it much better. Why should we curtail the number of hospitals and increase the number of beds in the "accredited" hospitals?
The experience in other countries where abortion was legalized justifies our attitude towards this amendment.
Recently, a paper published an article entitled: English concerned about abortion law.
Mr. Speaker, this article deals with the results of legalizing abortion in that country, I quote:
The current application of the act authorizing abortion under certain conditions causes "serious concern, even to the advocates of the act", stated Richard Crossman, British Minister for Social Services, Monday afternoon in the House of Commons.
The act, adopted by parliament in October 1967 and which became effective in April 1968, authorizes termination of a pregnancy when it threatens or harms the physical or the mental health of the mother, that of the child to be born or that of the other children.
Mr. Crossman said that he was particularly displeased with the way in which the act was interpreted and applied in the private sector. Since June 1968, 22,000 abortions have been performed, of which more than a third in private clinics. The others were performed in state hospitals and paid for by social welfare.
Mr. Speaker, the last paragraph of the article which I have just quoted gives one of the main reasons which prompts us to propose the amendment now under study.
One of the main reasons there have been as many as 22,000 abortions since June 1968, is the increased number of hospitals where abortion may be procured. It is one of the reasons why we want to decrease the number of "accredited" hospitals. For this purpose, we are using the nefarious experience of other countries, so that we will not have to blame ourselves for the same mistakes.
And it says further, and I quote:
-in which the act is interpreted and applied in the private sector.
